hero.subtitle: GreenMind analyzes plant bioelectrical signals to detect stress earlier and specifically improve cultivation strategies.

problem.title2: when the damage is already visible.
problem.description: Today, sensors monitor the environment — temperature, humidity, soil moisture. But not the plant itself. However, plants send out bioelectrical signals that indicate stress — often before external symptoms become visible.

solution.title: Understanding plant signals. Acting more specifically.
solution.description: GreenMind records bioelectrical signals directly on the plant and makes them usable for data-driven cultivation decisions.

earlyStress.title: Early stress detection
earlyStress.description: Bioelectrical signals can indicate drought, pest, and nutrient stress — aiming to identify problems before visible damage occurs.

dataPlanning.title: Data-driven yield planning
dataPlanning.description: Plant signals combined with environmental data enable new approaches for yield planning — data-driven instead of purely experience-based.

resources.title: Targeted resource usage
resources.description: When the plant signals what it needs, water and nutrients can be used as needed — lower consumption, better results.

howItWorks.title: From signal to recommendation.
howItWorks.description: Plants react to their environment with measurable electrical signals. GreenMind makes these signals visible and analyzable.

s1.title: Plant signal
s1.description: Plants generate electrical signals in response to changes in their environment — light, water, temperature, nutrients.

s2.title: Sensors
s2.description: Sensors on the plant capture these signals non-invasively and combine them with environmental data like temperature and soil moisture.

s3.title: Analysis
s3.description: The data is automatically processed, filtered, and examined for patterns — which signals indicate which stress?

s4.title: Recommendation
s4.description: Insights are translated into concrete action recommendations — when to water, when to fertilize, when to intervene.

foundation.title: Scientifically founded. Field-tested.
foundation.description: Developed in collaboration with FHNW and building on peer-reviewed research in plant electrophysiology.

i1.title: Early stress detection

Content.howWeCaptureAndProcessPlantBioelectrical: How we capture and process plant bioelectrical signals and turn them into useful insights for cultivation.
Content.plantsRespondToChangesInTheirEnvironment: Plants respond to changes in their environment with measurable electrical signals — including changes in light, water availability, temperature, nutrients and pest pressure. Scientific studies show that these signals contain information about stress that conventional environmental sensors cannot provide.
Content.greenmindRecordsTheseSignalsDirectlyFrom: GreenMind records these signals directly from the plant, continuously and non-invasively. Combined with environmental measurements such as temperature and soil moisture, they provide a broader picture of the plant's condition.
Content.sensorsAttachedToThePlantCaptureBioelect: Sensors attached to the plant capture bioelectrical signals alongside environmental measurements: temperature, light, humidity and soil moisture. All measurements are synchronized on a shared timeline.
Content.rawDataIsAutomaticallyFilteredNormalized: Raw data is automatically filtered, normalized and prepared as time series for analysis. Patterns and deviations are identified to support interpretation.
Content.signalPatternsAreComparedWithDocumentedS: Signal patterns are compared with documented stress events to study relationships between plant signals and actual conditions in the field.
Content.theSystemHasThreeLayersESP32BasedSensor: The system has three layers. ESP32-based sensor units collect data in the field and send it to Raspberry Pi gateways. The gateways store it locally and forward it to the central server. Local storage protects measurements during connection interruptions.
Content.communicationBetweenFieldGatewaysAndTheS: Communication between field gateways and the server is encrypted using HTTPS. Each gateway authenticates with its own API key.
Content.distinguishingTypesOfStressThroughBioele: Distinguishing types of stress through bioelectrical signals, including drought, pest pressure and nutrient deficiencies. The goal is automatic classification based on long-term observations.
Content.sensorsDesignedForRealConditionsHighHumi: Sensors designed for real conditions: high humidity, UV exposure, dust and temperature fluctuations from -5 °C to +50 °C.
Content.aScalablePipelineForContinuousAcquisitio: A scalable pipeline for continuous acquisition, processing and long-term storage of measurement data for longitudinal studies and controlled experiments.
Content.visualizeMeasurementDataAtAConfigurableR: Visualize measurement data at a configurable resolution, from raw data to daily averages, with synchronized charts and interactive time navigation.
Content.structuredCSVAndZIPExportsOfSensorData: Structured CSV and ZIP exports of sensor data for further analysis, with defined formats that support reproducibility.
Content.centralManagementOfMeasurementStationsWi: Central management of measurement stations, with connectivity monitoring, remote configuration and automatic reset when hardware is replaced.
Content.fromDataAcquisitionInTheFieldToAnalysis: From data acquisition in the field to analysis in the dashboard — the areas we are working on.
Content.peterSpentMoreThanTwoDecadesAsA: Peter spent more than two decades as a Research Scientist at the MIT Sloan School of Management and is an honorary professor at the University of Cologne. His current research at Galaxylabs.org focuses on well-being and human–animal and human–plant communication. With a PhD in computer science from the University of Zurich and postdoctoral research at MIT, he contributes expertise in collaborative intelligence and data-driven research to GreenMind.
Content.traverStudiesDataScienceAtFHNWAndCombine: Traver studies data science at FHNW and combines his studies with applied research at GreenMind. Having completed a Swiss vocational qualification as a physics laboratory technician at armasuisse, he brings experience in data analysis, electronics and sensing. He connects sensor hardware with data analysis and is responsible for platform development, sensor integration and the data pipeline.
Content.understandingPlantBioelectricalSignalsTo: Understanding plant bioelectrical signals to improve cultivation decisions.
Content.agricultureCurrentlyMonitorsTemperatureL: Agriculture currently monitors temperature, light and soil moisture, but rarely the condition of the plant itself. GreenMind aims to change that. We are developing a system that records plant bioelectrical signals to support better cultivation decisions. A Galaxyadvisors AG project in collaboration with FHNW.
Content.globalDemandForFoodIsRisingWhileWater: Global demand for food is rising, while water and farmland are under pressure. Climate variability makes conventional cultivation less predictable. Plants continuously produce electrical signals that can indicate stress, often before visible damage appears. GreenMind investigates how these signals can support better cultivation decisions.
Content.eachComponentIsTestedUnderRealCultivatio: Each component is tested under real cultivation conditions, in greenhouses and outdoors, together with FHNW and agricultural partners. We document our results in the Science Center and compare them with current scientific literature.
Content.ourTechnologyBuildsOnPeerReviewedResearc: Our technology builds on peer-reviewed research in plant electrophysiology. Explore the scientific foundations, from bioelectrical signals to data-driven stress classification.

Research.text1: Flexible organic multi-electrode arrays map Venus flytrap action potentials at high resolution. The study demonstrates precise, non-invasive measurement of plant bioelectrical signals, providing a technical foundation for GreenMind's sensing approach.
Research.text2: Development of conformable organic electrochemical transistor arrays (OECTs) for large-scale mapping of action potentials in plant tissue at high spatial and temporal resolution.
Research.text4: Peter Gloor shows that bioelectrical signals from a purple-heart plant can classify environmental conditions (85.4% accuracy) and human emotions (73%). The study demonstrates the potential of machine learning for analysing plant signals of the kind recorded by GreenMind.
Research.text5: Classification of environmental and emotional states using bioelectrical signals from Tradescantia pallida, recorded with an AD8232 sensor and analysed with CNN models.
Research.text7: Peter Gloor demonstrates measurable differences in plant bioelectrical activity when a person moves nearby. Random-forest classifiers achieve 62.7% accuracy on 2,978 samples across three plant species, providing further evidence that plant signals respond to environmental changes.
Research.text8: Bioelectrical recordings from 2,978 plant samples (basil, lettuce and tomato) are classified using random forest and CNN models to detect statistically significant differences between recordings with and without nearby human movement.
Research.text10: Electrical impedance measurements on plant stems detect water stress with up to 95% correlation with soil moisture. This low-cost approach measures plant needs directly, aligning with GreenMind's sensing approach.
Research.text11: In-vivo impedance measurements on plant stems show a significant correlation with environmental parameters, enabling direct, low-cost, live monitoring of plant condition without visual inspection.
Research.text12: Electrophysiological signals are used to detect nutrient deficiencies in greenhouse plants. This supports using the sensing approach behind GreenMind to investigate nutrient stress as well as water stress directly in plants.
Research.text13: Use of electrophysiological signals for advanced assessment of nutrient deficiencies in greenhouse environments.
Research.text14: This foundational study shows that plants respond to environmental stress through action and variation potentials, including responses to pests, pesticides and heavy metals. It provides a scientific basis for using plants as living biosensors, as explored by GreenMind.
Research.text15: Review of electrical signals as a means of using plants as rapid biosensors for light direction, insect attacks, pesticides, uncouplers and heavy-metal exposure.
Research.text16: A comprehensive review of methods for detecting heavy metals in plants, including non-invasive measurements. This is relevant to GreenMind because heavy-metal exposure affects plant biomarkers and electrical signals.
Research.text17: Systematic review of techniques for analysing and detecting heavy-metal concentrations in plants, including ICP-MS, XRF, non-invasive micro-tests and omics approaches.
Research.text18: Hedera helix is fitted with a PhytoNode wearable that records electrophysiological signals outdoors for five months. AutoML classifiers achieve an F1 score of up to 95%, demonstrating the potential of plant electrical signals for environmental monitoring under real conditions.
Research.text19: A biohybrid system with a plant-wearable device (PhytoNode) continuously records electrophysiological activity in Hedera helix. AutoML approaches outperform manual tuning, with an F1 score of up to 95%.
Research.text20: Machine-learning classifiers (random forest and SVC) distinguish stages of tomato ripening from electrophysiological signals with more than 80% accuracy. The study shows that the plant electrome, as recorded by GreenMind, can also reflect developmental processes in fruit.
Research.text21: Electrical activity in tomato fruit (Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme) is recorded as voltage variations during ripening and analysed using FFT, wavelets, PSD and approximate entropy. Machine-learning methods including random forest, SVC and KNN classify three ripening stages (mature green, breaker and light red) with up to 80.76% accuracy.
